transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi, nice to meet you too. Um, well, I’m here because... honestly, work has just become completely unmanageable lately. I’m a registered nurse, and I work on a really busy floor—which I used to love, you know, the fast pace and everything, I’ve got my graduate degree and I’ve always pushed myself to be on top of things—but lately, the main reason I’m here is that I just lose my train of thought constantly on the floor. Like, constantly. It’s actually getting kind of scary. 

I’ll be in the middle of figuring out a really complex patient flow issue, like trying to coordinate discharges and admissions or sorting out who needs to go where, and all it takes is one little thing to completely derail me. An IV pump starts beeping down the hall, or, you know, someone at the nurses' station asks another nurse a totally unrelated question about a chart or something, or a call light goes off three doors down. And it's like... poof. My brain just wipes completely blank. Suddenly I’m standing there and I have absolutely zero idea what I was just working on or what I was about to do. And in nursing, you really can't afford to just forget what you're doing, so I spend half my shift just trying to retrace my own steps because every single noise or interruption just completely pulls my attention away and I can't get it back.
Before all this got worse at work, did you have trouble with focus or distractibility as a child?

Yeah, actually, I really did. It’s funny you ask that because I was just talking to my mom about this recently when I was trying to figure out why I'm struggling so much now. I mean, if you look all the way back to elementary school, like second or third grade, it was always the exact same story. Every single parent-teacher conference, every report card, the teachers would always write these long notes saying that I was a really bright girl, that I had so much potential, but that I was just so... careless. That was the word they always used. Careless. 

Because I was just constantly losing things. I'd do a worksheet—like those spelling or math worksheets we always had—and I would actually do the work, or at least most of it, but then it would just vanish into the black hole of my desk or get completely crumpled up at the bottom of my backpack. Or I'd just completely forget to turn it in. I'd walk right past the homework tray in the morning. It was like there was a total disconnect between doing the assignment and actually finishing the process of handing it over. 

And it got to the point where my mom... bless her heart, she was working too, but she literally had to sit with me at the kitchen table every single night. Just to keep me on track. If she got up for even a second to stir a pot on the stove or answer the landline, I'd instantly be staring at the wall or peeling the paper off my crayons or just completely off in my own world. She had to sit right there, hovering over my shoulder, basically micromanaging my entire evening just so I could get through a basic half-hour assignment. It was exhausting for her, and honestly, it was frustrating for me because I wanted to just do it and go play, but I couldn't seem to stay focused unless she was right there acting like my... I don't know, my external brain. And even then, after all that effort of her sitting with me, I'd still somehow manage to lose the paper on the bus the next morning, which would just start the whole cycle over again...
Do these same attention problems affect you outside of work, like at home or in daily tasks?

Oh, absolutely. It’s not just work at all. It’s... honestly, it’s everything. It bleeds into every single part of my life, which is just so exhausting. Like, I’ll have these totally routine things that I need to do, things that a normal adult should just be able to handle without a second thought, and they just completely slip my mind. 

For instance, paying bills. You’d think that would be easy, right? You get a bill, you pay it. But I’ll get the electric bill in the mail, I’ll open it, I’ll look at it, and I’ll think, "Okay, I need to log in and pay this." And then maybe the dog barks, or I notice a spot on the counter that needs wiping, and... it’s gone. Completely gone from my brain. I’ve had my electricity shut off before, not because I didn’t have the money, but literally just because I forgot to click the button to pay it. And I’ll even try to outsmart myself, you know? I’ll set a reminder on my phone. "Pay electric bill at 6 PM." The alarm goes off at 6 PM, I look at it, I swipe it away thinking, "Okay, I’ll do that in exactly two minutes when I finish making this sandwich," and then... poof. Two weeks later, I’m sitting in the dark.

And it’s not just chores, it’s my relationships, too. My sister will call me and leave a voicemail, or text me to ask a quick question, and I’ll read it and think, "Oh, I need to call her back as soon as I finish this shift or as soon as I get home." And I genuinely mean to. I want to talk to her! But the thought just evaporates. Days will go by, and then she’ll text me again, clearly annoyed, asking if I’m ignoring her. And I feel so terrible because I’m not ignoring her, I just literally forgot she existed in that context for three days. 

Even appointments. I’ll schedule a dentist appointment six months in advance, write it on the calendar on the fridge, put it in my phone calendar, set a reminder for the day before... and I will still somehow manage to miss it. Because on the actual day, I’ll get distracted by something else in the morning, and suddenly it’s 3 PM and I was supposed to be in the chair at 1 PM. It’s like my brain just cannot hold onto these basic, everyday tasks, no matter how many safety nets I try to set up for myself. It’s just so incredibly frustrating to feel like I can’t even manage my own life outside of the hospital, let alone inside it.
Have these focus and forgetfulness problems been present pretty much your whole life?

Well, I mean, like I was just saying about the childhood stuff with my mom having to sit with me, that underlying scattered feeling has always kind of been there, humming in the background of my life. But it was never, ever this severe. I mean, I managed to get through nursing school, I got my graduate degree, I had all these little workarounds that kept me afloat. 

But this current situation? Where I feel like I'm completely losing my grip on reality? This has been a major problem since I took on the expanded charge-nurse responsibilities almost two years ago. It’ll be exactly two years this fall, actually. Because before that, I was just a regular floor nurse. I had my specific patients for the shift, usually just three or four, and I could just zero in on them. I had my checklist, I had my routine, and I could handle it. 

But then our unit manager pulled me into her office and gave me this whole speech about how I had my master's now and I was such a strong clinician, and they really needed someone to step up and take over the charge role for the day shift. And of course, I was flattered, so I said yes. But I had no idea what I was actually agreeing to. Suddenly, I’m not just managing my own assignment, I’m managing the entire floor. I'm doing the staffing matrix for the next shift, I'm fielding back-to-back calls from the ER about incoming admissions, I'm tracking which of our thirty-two beds is being cleaned by environmental services, I'm dealing with pharmacy delays, I'm stepping in when family members are upset... all at the exact same time. 

It’s just... it's like someone opened a hundred tabs in my brain and then froze the computer. Ever since I took that on, almost two years ago, it's just been this massive, snowballing disaster. I kept telling myself, "Oh, you just need a few months to adjust to the new role, everyone gets overwhelmed at first," but it's been two years. Two years of just constantly dropping the ball. And because my brain is so completely fried by the end of my shift from trying to juggle all those expanded duties, I have absolutely nothing left for my actual life when I clock out, which is why the bills and the appointments and my sister are all just falling through the cracks now...
Do you spend a lot of time worrying about many different things, even when there isn’t an immediate problem to solve?

Worrying? Um... no, not really. I mean, not in the sense of just sitting around agonizing over things when everything is actually fine. I know some people do that, like they just spin out over the "what ifs" or borrow trouble from the future, worrying about things that haven't even happened yet or might never happen at all. 

But for me, it's... well, I don't really have the luxury of worrying about things that aren't immediate problems, because I feel like I am constantly drowning in actual, tangible, immediate problems. The things I get stressed out about are the very real, very concrete things that I am currently messing up or forgetting right in that moment. Like, I'm not sitting at home worrying "oh, what if something bad happens next week." I'm stressing because I know I forgot to update the staffing matrix at work, or I'm stressing because I know I was supposed to call my sister back three days ago and I still haven't done it and now she's mad at me. It's always tied directly to a ball I've actually dropped. 

My brain is just so incredibly consumed with trying to keep up with the sheer chaos of my actual, current reality that there's just no room left to invent things to worry about, if that makes sense? I'm basically just trying to survive the next ten minutes of my shift, or trying to remember what I walked into the kitchen for, so sitting around worrying about random possibilities or abstract things just isn't really something I do. It's just the overwhelming weight of the things I'm actively failing to manage that gets to me, not really... generalized worry.
Have you been feeling down or depressed most days?

Down or depressed? Um... no. Not really. I mean, I know what depression looks like, right? Being a nurse, I see it all the time. You see patients who just can't get out of bed, who have that flat affect, who just feel this heavy, pervasive sadness or emptiness that colors every single thing they do. And that’s... that's really not me at all. 

I don't wake up feeling hopeless or sad. Actually, it's almost the exact opposite? I wake up almost every single morning feeling like, "Okay, today is the day! Today I'm going to be organized, today I'm going to get my shift assignments done early, today I'm going to remember to pay that bill!" I have all this motivation and good intention when I start my day. I really do want to do things and I look forward to things. 

It's just that by, like, 2 PM, when I've lost my clipboard for the third time and I realize I never sent that email to the pharmacy that I drafted at 8 AM... *then* I feel bad. But it's not depression, it's just... profound frustration. I get so mad at myself. I feel defeated because I keep trying so incredibly hard and I just keep failing at these basic things. So, sure, I have moments where I want to go cry in the clean supply closet because I'm just so completely overwhelmed by everything I'm dropping, but it's always a direct reaction to me messing up, you know? It's not this dark cloud that follows me around for no reason. 

If I actually have a good day where I manage to keep my head above water, or if I'm just at home on a day off and I don't have a million demands being thrown at me, my mood is totally fine. I can laugh, I can enjoy things. So, no, I wouldn't say I feel down or depressed most days. I'm just... really, really tired of feeling incompetent. But the sadness is just frustration, really.
Do you often feel restless, like it’s hard to sit still?

Restless? Like, physically can't sit still? No, not really. I mean, I'm a nurse, so I'm on my feet for twelve hours a day anyway, constantly walking from room to room, going to the Pyxis machine, running to the supply closet, walking down to the ER to get a report... so I don't really have the opportunity to just sit and realize I can't sit still, if that makes sense? 

But even when I am home, like on my days off, I don't feel that physical urge to move. Like, I don't tap my foot, I don't bounce my leg, I don't feel like I have a motor running inside me. I see that sometimes in my pediatric patients, you know, the ones who literally cannot stay in the chair, they're climbing the exam table, they're touching everything. That's not me. 

Actually, when I finally do get to sit down at the end of the day, I just kind of... crash. I'll sit on the couch and just completely zone out because I'm so physically and mentally exhausted from the shift. I can definitely sit still for hours if I'm watching a movie or something, assuming I don't get distracted by my phone or remember a chore I forgot to do. So it's more like my *brain* is restless, constantly jumping from one thought to the next, but my body is perfectly fine staying put. I don't have that physical hyperactivity at all. I'm just tired, mostly. Really tired.

It's not this dark cloud that follows me around for no reason. 

If I actually have a good day where I manage to keep my head above water, or if I'm just at home on a day off and I don't have a million demands being thrown at me, my mood is totally fine. I can laugh, I can enjoy things. So, no, I wouldn't say I feel down or depressed most days. I'm just... really, really tired of feeling incompetent. But the sadness is just frustration, really.

inference.note: Ruled out F32.A and G31.84 based on absence of persistent depressed mood and lifelong attention symptoms starting in childhood rather than later-life cognitive decline. Ongoing impairment across settings with childhood onset strongly supports F90.0; stress-related worsening in the expanded charge role keeps F43.23 as a secondary possibility.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there are core hyperactivity/impulsivity symptoms, which would further support ADHD rather than an adjustment-related condition.
doctor.question: Do you often feel restless, like it’s hard to sit still?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feelings of restlessness or difficulty sitting still, which corresponds to hyperactivity symptoms like 'Often fidgets with or taps hands or feet or squirms in seat' or 'Often feels restless'. These symptoms are not present in my profile.

patient.answer:
Restless? Like, physically can't sit still? No, not really. I mean, I'm a nurse, so I'm on my feet for twelve hours a day anyway, constantly walking from room to room, going to the Pyxis machine, running to the supply closet, walking down to the ER to get a report... so I don't really have the opportunity to just sit and realize I can't sit still, if that makes sense? 

But even when I am home, like on my days off, I don't feel that physical urge to move. Like, I don't tap my foot, I don't bounce my leg, I don't feel like I have a motor running inside me. I see that sometimes in my pediatric patients, you know, the ones who literally cannot stay in the chair, they're climbing the exam table, they're touching everything. That's not me. 

Actually, when I finally do get to sit down at the end of the day, I just kind of... crash. I'll sit on the couch and just completely zone out because I'm so physically and mentally exhausted from the shift. I can definitely sit still for hours if I'm watching a movie or something, assuming I don't get distracted by my phone or remember a chore I forgot to do. So it's more like my *brain* is restless, constantly jumping from one thought to the next, but my body is perfectly fine staying put. I don't have that physical hyperactivity at all. I'm just tired, mostly. Really tired.

inference.note: Chronic childhood-onset inattentive symptoms across settings remain strongly supported; generalized anxiety and depressive features are not endorsed, and there is no prominent adjustment-related mood/anxiety syndrome beyond frustration secondary to attentional impairment. Hyperactivity is absent, consistent with predominantly inattentive presentation.
